core: 'New Imperialism' (c. 1870-1914): an intense, industrial-era wave in which industrial powers (Britain, France, Germany, Belgium, Italy, Portugal, Russia, and later the United States and Japan) conquered most of Africa and much of Asia, distinguished from earlier colonization by its speed, scale, and industrial technology

Motives: economic (raw materials such as rubber, ivory, minerals, palm oil; new markets; capital investment); strategic/nationalist competition for prestige and military dominance over rivals; and ideological justification via the racist 'civilizing mission' (Christianity, commerce, civilization) based on assumptions of White superiority
The 'civilizing mission' must be presented as the imperialists' rationalization for conquest and profit, not as an accurate account of colonialism's effects

The Scramble for Africa: European control of Africa rose from about 10% to about 90% between the start of the Second Industrial Revolution and 1914; by 1914 only Ethiopia (Abyssinia) and Liberia remained independent

The Berlin Conference, 15 November 1884 to 26 February 1885, convened by German Chancellor Otto von Bismarck; 14 states attended (13 European powers plus the United States); NO African representatives were present; it set rules for partition, notably the 'effective occupation' principle

Methods of imperial control: coerced treaties with local rulers, military conquest with industrial weapons, indirect rule through protectorates governing via existing elites, and economic extraction (cash crops, mineral/rubber extraction, infrastructure built to export raw materials rather than serve local needs)

The Congo Free State (1885-1908) was the personal private possession of King Leopold II of Belgium (not the Belgian government), run for profit behind humanitarian pretenses; its forced-labor rubber and ivory system used beatings, hostage-taking, and mutilation including the severing of hands; death-toll estimates range from at least one million to about ten million Congolese; international exposure (Casement report, Congo Reform Association) forced Belgium to annex it in 1908

Resistance and agency of colonized peoples: widespread revolts and armed defense; Ethiopia decisively defeated Italy at the Battle of Adwa on 1 March 1896 under Emperor Menelik II, preserving its independence
Legacies: arbitrary externally-drawn borders, extraction-oriented economies and dependence, embedded racial hierarchies, and the provocation of national movements that later drove decolonization
supporting: The Second Industrial Revolution gave a few industrial powers decisive advantages in weapons, steamships, railways, medicine (quinine), and communications, enabling deep projection of power into Africa and Asia

The Battle of Adwa arose from the disputed 1889 Treaty of Wuchale (Wichale): Italy claimed a protectorate via Article 17 while Menelik II rejected that reading; Italy was commanded by General Oreste Baratieri and suffered roughly 6,000 dead and about 3,000 captured, described as the worst defeat of a European army in the history of colonialism; Italy then recognized Ethiopian independence
Berlin Conference rationale of the 'effective occupation' principle accelerated rather than restrained conquest by requiring physical control to validate a claim
The Congo Free State was roughly 80 times larger than Belgium and by 1901 produced about 10% of the world's rubber

claims.claim: The 'New Imperialism' of roughly 1870-1914 was driven by economic motives (raw materials, markets, investment), strategic/nationalist competition for prestige and military dominance, and an ideological 'civilizing mission' resting on assumptions of White superiority.
The 'civilizing mission' was an imperialist rationalization for conquest and profit, based on ingrained assumptions of White superiority, not an accurate description of colonialism's effects.
During the Scramble for Africa, European control of the continent rose from about 10 percent to roughly 90 percent, and by 1914 only Ethiopia and Liberia remained independent.

The Berlin Conference ran from 15 November 1884 to 26 February 1885, was convened by Otto von Bismarck, was attended by fourteen states (thirteen European powers plus the United States), included no African representatives, and set rules for partition such as 'effective occupation.'

The Congo Free State (1885-1908) was the personal private possession of King Leopold II of Belgium, whose forced-labor rubber and ivory system used mutilation including the severing of hands and caused mass death, with estimates ranging from at least one million to about ten million Congolese; international exposure led Belgium to annex it in 1908.

On 1 March 1896 at the Battle of Adwa, Ethiopian forces under Emperor Menelik II decisively defeated an invading Italian army under General Baratieri, inflicting about 6,000 dead and taking around 3,000 prisoners, and Italy was forced to recognize Ethiopia's independence.

Imperial powers controlled colonies through coerced treaties, military conquest, indirect rule via protectorates, and economic extraction, with infrastructure built primarily to export raw materials rather than to benefit local populations.

Imperialism left long-term legacies including arbitrary externally-drawn borders, extraction-oriented dependent economies, and embedded racial hierarchies, and it provoked the resistance and national movements that later drove decolonization.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Death toll of the Congo Free State
positions: World History Encyclopedia: 'at least one million Africans died... some historians would put the figure at 10 million'
Widely cited estimates put the toll at roughly ten million, around half the population, between 1885 and 1908; some historians dispute the highest figures and the demographic baseline
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the toll as a range (at least one million to about ten million) attributed to historians' estimates, presents the atrocities as established fact, and avoids asserting a single contested figure as exact.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the Congo catastrophe constitutes genocide
positions: Some scholars call it genocide or a 'holocaust'
Others argue it was rapacious economic exploitation that produced mass death as a consequence rather than a documented policy of extermination
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson describes the documented atrocities and mass death factually without adjudicating the genocide-label debate, which is not required for the topic's scope.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft was pure boilerplate ('Imperialism is a foundational concept in History... a simple way to apply it') with no substantive historical content, dates, or examples. None of it was reused.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the placeholder definition and generic vocabulary with a substantive treatment of the New Imperialism, its motives, the Berlin Conference, the Congo Free State, Adwa, and legacies.
Added verified dates (Berlin Conference 15 Nov 1884-26 Feb 1885; Adwa 1 March 1896; Congo Free State 1885-1908) and figures (10%-90% of Africa; ~6,000 Italian dead / ~3,000 captured at Adwa).
Framed the 'civilizing mission' explicitly as an imperialist rationalization, and centered the agency and resistance of colonized peoples per the subject's center-the-colonized control.
